We are given

\[
f(x)=
\begin{cases}
x^2+1, & x \text{ irrational},\\[2mm]
\tan x, & x \text{ rational},
\end{cases}
\qquad x\in[0,4\pi].
\]

We need the number of points in \([0,4\pi]\) where \(f\) is continuous.

---

### 1. Continuity criterion

The rationals and irrationals are both dense in \([0,4\pi]\). Therefore, for \(f\) to be continuous at a point \(a\), the two pieces must approach the same finite limit as \(x\to a\).

For any \(a\) that is not a pole of \(\tan x\), we have

\[
\lim_{\substack{x\to a\\ x\in\mathbb Q}} f(x)=\tan a,
\]

and

\[
\lim_{\substack{x\to a\\ x\notin\mathbb Q}} f(x)=a^2+1.
\]

Thus \(f\) can be continuous at \(a\) only if

\[
\tan a=a^2+1.
\]

If this equality holds, then both dense branches approach the same value, and \(f(a)\) also equals that value, so \(f\) is continuous at \(a\).

At the poles of \(\tan x\), namely

\[
x=\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{3\pi}{2},\frac{5\pi}{2},\frac{7\pi}{2},
\]

the rational values of \(\tan x\) become unbounded, so \(f\) is not continuous there.

So the continuity points are exactly the solutions of

\[
\tan x=x^2+1
\]

in \([0,4\pi]\).

---

### 2. Counting solutions of \(\tan x=x^2+1\)

Since

\[
x^2+1>0,
\]

any solution must satisfy

\[
\tan x>0.
\]

In \([0,4\pi]\), \(\tan x>0\) only on the intervals

\[
[0,\tfrac{\pi}{2}),\quad
(\pi,\tfrac{3\pi}{2}),\quad
(2\pi,\tfrac{5\pi}{2}),\quad
(3\pi,\tfrac{7\pi}{2}).
\]

We show that there is exactly one solution in each of these four intervals.

Define

\[
h(x)=\tan x-(x^2+1).
\]

A solution of \(\tan x=x^2+1\) is a zero of \(h\).

---

### 3. First interval: \([0,\pi/2)\)

We have

\[
h(0)=\tan 0-(0^2+1)=-1<0,
\]

and

\[
\lim_{x\to(\pi/2)^-}h(x)=+\infty.
\]

So there is at least one zero.

Now

\[
h'(x)=\sec^2 x-2x.
\]

For \(0<x<\pi/2\), we know \(\tan x>x\). Hence

\[
\sec^2 x=1+\tan^2 x>1+x^2\ge 2x,
\]

so

\[
h'(x)>0.
\]

Thus \(h\) is strictly increasing on \([0,\pi/2)\), so it has exactly one zero there.

---

### 4. Other positive-tangent intervals

Consider

\[
I_k=(k\pi,k\pi+\tfrac{\pi}{2}),\qquad k=1,2,3.
\]

On each such interval,

\[
h(k\pi)=-(k\pi)^2-1<0,
\]

and

\[
\lim_{x\to(k\pi+\pi/2)^-}h(x)=+\infty.
\]

So each \(I_k\) contains at least one zero.

Now examine monotonicity. We have

\[
h'(x)=\sec^2 x-2x,
\]

and

\[
h''(x)=2\sec^2 x\tan x-2.
\]

On \(I_k\), \(\tan x>0\). Let

\[
\phi(x)=\sec^2 x\tan x.
\]

Then

\[
\phi'(x)=\sec^4 x+2\sec^2 x\tan^2 x>0,
\]

so \(\phi\) is strictly increasing from \(0\) to \(+\infty\) on \(I_k\). Therefore \(h''\) has exactly one zero on \(I_k\), meaning \(h'\) decreases once and then increases.

Also,

\[
h'(k\pi)=1-2k\pi<0,
\]

while

\[
\lim_{x\to(k\pi+\pi/2)^-}h'(x)=+\infty.
\]

Thus \(h'\) has exactly one zero on \(I_k\). Hence \(h\) decreases once and then increases. Since it starts negative and ends at \(+\infty\), it crosses zero exactly once on each \(I_k\).

Therefore there is exactly one solution in each of the intervals

\[
(\pi,\tfrac{3\pi}{2}),\quad
(2\pi,\tfrac{5\pi}{2}),\quad
(3\pi,\tfrac{7\pi}{2}).
\]

---

### 5. Total number of continuity points

There is exactly one solution in each of the four intervals

\[
[0,\tfrac{\pi}{2}),\quad
(\pi,\tfrac{3\pi}{2}),\quad
(2\pi,\tfrac{5\pi}{2}),\quad
(3\pi,\tfrac{7\pi}{2}),
\]

and none elsewhere. Hence \(f\) is continuous at exactly

\[
\boxed{4}
\]

points in \([0,4\pi]\).
